When discussing concerns regarding data use, she brings her hands closer together, forming a more closed and protective gesture.
qAndA.question: How does Marjolijn Antheunis use her hands to emphasize her points?

qAndA.answer: The overall mood of the video is thoughtful and contemplative. The video presents a balanced view of social media, acknowledging both its benefits and drawbacks, prompting viewers to critically engage with the ethical implications of its use.

qAndA.answer: Her main argument is that leaving social media is not a practical solution due to its many benefits. Instead, she advocates for stronger regulations to protect user data and increased user awareness regarding data sharing.
qAndA.question: What is the main argument Marjolijn Antheunis presents in response to the question about leaving social media to protect data and privacy?

timecoded_text_to_speech.text: I don't think that is a solution.
I think Facebook has put a lot of other social media platforms,
which gives us a lot of benefits, especially for our social network.
It's very easy to maintain our social network, via social media.
But nothing is for free in this world.
It's also not Facebook or Instagram or Snapchat.
We use it for free.
It don't cost us any money.
But it costs us data.
They use our data.
And that is known since the early days of Facebook and all the other platforms.
So if you don't like that, then you can leave Facebook or social media.
But then I would advise you to stay away from the internet as much as possible,
because also using Google gives Google a lot of data and they use it.
They do it already for many years and they will do it even more in the future.
At least our studies show that we do not become more or less happy.
So this does not have any effect on happiness.
But it has some social effects on social capital.
We have found that in our research, but also a lot of studies in the US
found that if you use social media, it benefits your social capital.
And we also found a few effects on social competence.
And that's especially early and lessons who are using Facebook.
They get more social competence, not only online, but also offline.
On the one hand, there should be regulations.
There are regulations, by the way, but for the normal use of our data
for commercial purposes for advertising, there are regulations.
And in these regulations, it's also said that what happened with Cambridge
and the LITICA is not good.
So in fact, it should be tested more.
And I think that is a task for the government.
On the other hand, I think we, as users, should be aware that our data is used.
We cannot use it for free without that the company uses our data.
That's impossible.
So, or we should accept that we have to pay a fee every month.
And then they cannot do those things.
That's one thing.
Or if we know it's for free and they use our data,
we should be very much aware of what we post online.
And we realize that we have to pay for it.
And then we can ask them not to use our data.
But still, the control is something.
Of course, you expect that the ethical consciousness
and the moral of the company is good enough,
but in the end, it's all about the money.
So we should not leave it to the company alone.
There should be more parties, stakeholders involved.
Yeah.

youtube_description:
'Leave Facebook? Then better leave internet altogether' says Prof. Communication & Technologies, Marjolijn Antheunis, Tilburg School of Humanities and Digital Sciences.

The interview is an introduction to Debatable, organized by Academic Forum: 'Life after Facebook?', which is held on the 24th of April 2018 Academic Forum  organizes: 
https://www.tilburguniversity.edu/campus/academic-forum/show/Debatable-Facebook-.htm

April 19 2018
